name: Gokarna Mahabaleshwara Temple
deity: Shiva as Mahabaleshwara, worshipped as the Atmalinga
period: Ancient teertha of the epics; temple rebuilt through the medieval centuries
summary: On the Arabian Sea coast of Karnataka, Gokarna is among the most sacred of Shiva shrines — home to the Atmalinga, the very "soul-linga" of Shiva, which legend says was set here forever when Ravana was tricked into laying it down.

sections.history: Gokarna is one of the oldest and holiest Shiva kshetras of the west coast, its sanctity praised in the epics and Puranas and counted by tradition among the great teerthas, comparable to Kashi. The seaside town, set between two rivers where they meet the Arabian Sea, grew around the shrine of Mahabaleshwara, patronised across the Kadamba and later dynasties and rebuilt over the medieval centuries. Long a centre of Vedic learning as well as pilgrimage, Gokarna has drawn devotees to its shore for the worship of Shiva and for the rites owed to ancestors.
sections.architecture: The temple, in the Dravidian manner with the timber-and-tile features of the Karnataka coast, enshrines the Atmalinga within its sanctum — a linga worshipped as the Pranalinga, the soul-linga of Shiva himself, seen by devotees only at certain times through the year. Stone halls and a spacious courtyard front the sea town, and close by run the sacred bathing spots at the meeting of river and ocean. The setting — temple, town, and the long sandy beaches beyond — makes Gokarna at once a place of intense pilgrimage and of the open coast.
sections.legends: Gokarna’s great legend is that of the Atmalinga. Ravana won from Shiva the soul-linga, all-powerful so long as it never touched the ground, and set out to carry it to Lanka; the gods, fearing his invincibility, sent Ganesha in the form of a boy. When Ravana paused for his evening prayers and entrusted the linga to the boy, Ganesha set it down, and it rooted to the earth forever — Mahabala, "the mighty one," which even Ravana could not lift. The name Gokarna, "cow’s ear," recalls Shiva’s emergence from the ear of the earth-cow; here the soul of Shiva is held in the stone.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is Gokarna’s supreme festival, when a great temple car is drawn through the town and pilgrims throng the shore, and the rare darshan of the Atmalinga is offered. Being a pre-eminent teertha, Gokarna is also thronged for ancestral rites and ritual bathing at the sea, especially on new-moon and eclipse days. Through the year the town keeps the double rhythm of a working pilgrimage centre and a stretch of open Konkan coast.
sections.experience: Gokarna offers a pilgrimage where temple and sea are inseparable. Devotees bathe where the river meets the ocean, then walk barefoot through the old town’s lanes to stand before the Atmalinga. The shrine’s intensity gives way, a few steps beyond, to long empty beaches under the Konkan sky — a rare meeting of deep sanctity and open coast that has made Gokarna beloved of pilgrims and wanderers alike. Dawn worship, the sound of the sea, and the knowledge of standing where Shiva’s own soul is enshrined lend the place a quiet power.

visit.timings: Generally open from around 6:00 am to 12:30 pm and 5:00 pm to 8:30 pm daily; hours extend during Maha Shivaratri and other festivals.
visit.dressCode: Traditional dress is required for the sanctum: men often worship bare-chested with a dhoti, and women in sarees or salwar kameez; shoulders and knees covered, footwear removed.
visit.photography: Photography is generally not permitted inside the temple; follow posted rules and staff guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Gokarna is in Uttara Kannada district on the coast, with its own small railway station on the Konkan Railway; Gokarna Road and Kumta are nearby railheads, and the nearest airports are Hubballi and Goa (Dabolim).
